To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified a new protein that is a component of the cilia of photoreceptors and that it is the first protein that is known to be specifically associated with the photoreceptor ciliary axonemes.
we identified a protein that interacts with RPGR, is expressed in the photoreceptors, and localizes specifically in the connecting cilium.

1) RPGRIP is expressed specifically in photoreceptors; 2) it is a structural protein that localizes to the connecting cilium; 3) it is stably associated in the ciliary axoneeme independent of RP; 4) it anchors RPGR in the cilium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the function of a protein that may be important in the pathogenesis of RP and may provide new insights into the function of the connecting cilium.
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying photoreceptor ciliogenesis and the pathogenesis of retinitis pigmentosis.
the identification and characterization of proteins that interact with the retinitis pigmentose GTPase regulator.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RPGRIP, a novel protein expressed specifically in the phototransduction apparatus of photoreceptors, is stably associated to the connecting cilium and anchors RPGR within this organelle.
RPGRIP, a protein that interacts with and is stably associated to the photoreceptor ciliary axonem, is a candidate gene that may play a role in photoreceptor ciliopathies.

the protein RPGRIP, a novel photoreceptor-specific protein with a C-terminal domain that binds RPGR, is stably associated in vivo with the photoreceptor cilium and is resistant to detergent extraction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identify a new photoreceptor protein that is localized to the connecting cilium, and that it is stably associated to the axonemal cytoskeleton.
RPGRIP may be a structural protein of the ciliary microtubule, and that it is a potential anchor for RPGR within the connecting cilium.
RPGRIP and RPGR are both expressed in rod and cone cilia, that RPGRIP interacts with RPGR and that RPGRIP may be a structural component of photoreceptor cilia that anchors RPGR to this organelle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RPGRIP may be a structural component of ciliary axonemes.
RPGRIP appears to anchor RPGR to the cilium.
